$comment: Startup contract for JanetHome. See DESIGN-NOTES.md section 1. Every entry either resolves or startup fails loudly. Do not soften onMissing.
$comment.mcpAuth: The ONE setting for how both local MCP servers treat the bearer token: require (anything but the right token is 401, and janet-mcp refuses to start without one), report (everything goes through; outcomes are counted on /health) or off (no check; the loopback guard still runs). Every launcher reads this key and passes it as --auth: Ensure-McpServer.ps1 (both run entries), ServerRotation.cs's targets, and ServerLink.cs when the CLI starts a janet-mcp. Staged cutover, 2026-10-21: report first, require once Claude Code is confirmed sending the header from its headersHelper (janet mcp-headers) -- read the counters in GET /health's 'auth' to confirm. Confirmed and flipped to require the same day: after a session restart, each Claude Code call moved ok +1 with missing unchanged on both servers. To flip: change this value, then rotate both servers so they restart with it. Decision record: thread item 65.
$comment.read: Kept to what the session cannot retrieve, because the read list is billed on EVERY start while the graph is billed only when asked. PROVENANCE.md left on 2026-08-08: its contract is already the boundary rule below, its detail is file.provenance, and its own manifest reason said 'read before adding anything' -- conditional by its own description, which is the definition of retrievable. README is the bootstrap: it must survive alone, because it is what tells the session the graph exists.

read.why: Bootstrap: how to start, the boundary, and that research.json is the entry point for everything else
The transferable patterns. Operating rules live here, not in a system prompt

$comment.run.threadReport: The key is 'threadReport', NOT the 'threadStack' it was until 2026-08-14, and the rename is deliberate: the envelope changed shape, so a consumer reading items[].notes would find the field simply absent and could reasonably conclude the item has no notes. A renamed key fails to resolve, which is loud; a same-named key holding a different shape is the quiet degradation this file exists to prevent. Show returned 174,129 characters on this machine's list -- past what an MCP tool result will even carry -- against 26,613 for the report, and three items held a third of it. The report answers 'where was I'; the notes are fetched per item once you know which one. 'threadStack' was already a misnomer besides: it stopped being a stack on 2026-08-08. Since 2026-09-04 the entry passes -Area through 'args', so the brief carries THIS repo's items only -- 67 open items across four repos had grown the report to 38,058 of the brief's 42,241 characters -- and the envelope's 'areas' map (report contract 3) names every other area with its open count, so the rest of the machine's backlog is summarised rather than dropped. The area is a manifest VALUE, not a constant in any script. It was the literal 'JanetHome' for a few hours on 2026-09-04, which narrowed the brief to the wrong repo: Start-Janet's own documented usual case is loading Janet WHILE WORKING SOMEWHERE ELSE, and a session in RazorGraphTool got nine JanetHome items in full with its own two as a bare count. Now it is the {projectName} token, substituted from -ProjectDir (Start-Janet passes its -Path), so the value still lives here and still says 'this session's repo' -- it just resolves per session instead of naming one repo forever. Any other {token} is a startup problem, because an unresolved one would reach -Area as a literal and return the empty list of an area nothing is filed under. A per-repo manifest was the alternative and was rejected: one value differs and everything else -- read entries, rules, retrieval -- would have been duplicated per repo, which is the drift this file exists to prevent.
$comment.run: Ensure-McpServer runs FIRST: it is the only entry whose failure silently removes capability rather than producing a wrong answer. A session whose server is down does not fail -- .mcp.json names a URL, so the tools are simply absent and the session falls back to the CLI, which works. That is the quiet degradation this contract exists to catch, one layer below where the contract used to look. It reports SERVED vs DECLARED tool counts because a server being up is not the same as a server being current: on 2026-08-14 the installed server answered with three tools while source declared twelve, and both global tools have reported 0.1.0 since the port, so the version could not tell them apart. Its failure is captured as a run 'error', never fatal -- the CLI fallback is real, and refusing to launch over a missing convenience would be worse than the fault.

run.why: Nothing else starts the janet-mcp HTTP server -- the transport is a separate process the client dials, which is what lets it be rebuilt mid-session and also what means no component owns starting it. Check 'ok' and 'stale' in the captured result before trusting that the research_* and thread_* tools are present

This repo's .mcp.json declares razorgraph on 7718 as well as janet on 7717, so a session here depends on both -- but until 2026-08-31 startup ensured only janet, and razorgraph's tools could be silently absent with every startup gate green. Same contract as the entry above: check 'ok' and 'stale' before trusting the razorgraph tools are present. These args are razorgraph's launch defaults and this is the only place they live: Invoke-GraphGuard.ps1 re-runs this entry by its captureAs when the server is down. razorgraph-mcp takes no --base (it is told which solution to graph per call), the port appears twice because the server is told it too, and Ensure-McpServer.ps1 appends --auth from mcpAuth. Until 2026-10-22 this was Ensure-RazorGraphServer.ps1, a forwarder carrying the same values, written when 'cmd' had nowhere to put arguments

Unfinished investigations from the last session: topics, focus, and note SIZES. Small, stateful, and useless if fetched late -- so it runs at startup rather than on demand. Narrowed by 'args' to the area named by the session's own project directory -- read the run entry's resolved 'args' in the brief to see which area that was -- and without notesLead -- narrowing alone left the brief at 9,969 characters against a budget of about 8,000; the envelope's 'areas' maps every other area's open count, so read that before assuming the items here are the whole backlog, and read one item's notes with thread_show or Show-ThreadItems.ps1 once you know which one you want

Startup validates the manifest's own entries; this validates the config files a session actually depends on -- drive-absolute paths in .mcp.json commands and settings.json permission rules -- and proposes replacements by deepest shared suffix. Captured, never a problem: it fires legitimately from a foreign project dir, and Start-Janet gates launch on problems (the 2026-08-01 regression). Read 'broken' in the captured result; it reports and proposes, never rewrites

$comment.retrieval: The tool inventory is deliberately NOT loaded here. research.json holds every script, pattern, note, and file as a node; startup carries only the pointer below and the session pulls the two or three nodes it needs. See DESIGN-NOTES section 2.

retrieval.$comment.via: 'via' stays a path because startup resolves it and a broken pointer must fail loudly. The script is now a thin shim over the same code the MCP server and the CLI run, so it is still a correct answer -- just no longer the only one. 'tools' below names the other two. Do not put a tool name here: it would stop resolving, and startup would report a problem that is not one.
retrieval.tools: Three front ends over one implementation (Janet.Core), so they cannot disagree: the research_query / research_add / research_update / research_rename MCP tools; 'janet research query|add|update|rename' on the command line; and the scripts, which now shim to the CLI. Use the MCP tools when they are connected -- no process start, and the schema is typed. Hooks and other shell callers need the CLI, which is why it is not optional.
retrieval.hint: Run it with no arguments for kinds and tags; -Query for scored search, -Tag / -Id for exact lookup, -? for the full surface. Responses report their own truncation. The research_* MCP tools are the same code.
retrieval.$comment.hint: 'hint' is the only prose from this block that reaches the trimmed brief. The fields below are reference material, emitted under -Full -- keep them accurate, but do not grow 'hint'. See notes\startup-brief-budget.md.
retrieval.$comment.json: These scripts emit compressed JSON by default -- the consumer is a model, not a terminal. Node boundaries are unambiguous, new schema fields arrive without a formatter change, and nothing is spent on alignment no reader uses. -Text opts into the formatted view; -Pretty indents the JSON for debugging.
usage: Get-Research.ps1                          -- kinds and tag index only (cheap orientation)
Get-Research.ps1 -Query 'thread stack'    -- scored top 5. -First N / -All to widen
Get-Research.ps1 -Id pattern.thread-items -Expand  -- a node plus its linked neighbours
Get-Research.ps1 -Kind script             -- every node of a kind
Add -Text for a human-readable form at the terminal; -Pretty to indent the JSON.
retrieval.envelope: Queries return { returned, totalMatches, truncated, nodes[] } -- check 'truncated' before concluding you have seen everything. An empty result uses the same shape, so never special-case it.
retrieval.add: research_add, 'janet research add', or scripts\Add-ResearchNode.ps1 -Id <kind>.<slug> -Kind <kind> -NodePath <path> -Summary '<one line>' -Tags a,b -Links id1,id2 -Caveats 'what bites you'. Validates and splices; never hand-edit research.json. -DryRun to preview.
retrieval.update: research_update, 'janet research update', or scripts\Update-ResearchNode.ps1 -Id <id> [-Summary|-Tags|-Links|-Caveats|-ScriptParams ...] [-Append] [-Remove field]. Preserves every field you do not name, including ones it has never heard of. Returns the before/after of each change. -DryRun to preview.
retrieval.caveats: Nodes may carry a 'caveats' array -- missing dependencies, external services, platform limits, outright breakage. Retrieval always prints them prefixed with '!'. Read them before relying on a node; several scripts in this repo are known-broken and say so.
retrieval.fallback: scripts\Get-ScriptCatalog.ps1 scans the script directory directly, for when a lookup misses or research.json is stale

$comment.rules: ENFORCED rules are backed by a mechanism that fails: startup validation, a hook that denies the tool call, or a linter that exits 1. ADVISORY rules hold only as long as the agent chooses to honour them -- they are marked so, because a rule claiming enforcement it does not have is worse than an honest suggestion. Do not rationalise past an advisory rule on the grounds that this particular case is small; that is the exact failure these were written after.
$comment.rules.enforcedBy: A rule claiming ENFORCED may carry 'enforcedBy': the hook script that backs it, as the hook itself resolves it -- Join-Path <project dir> <enforcedBy>. Startup tests that path against the CURRENT project dir (CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR, else cwd), because that is the only place the hook will look, AND requires a settings file the harness loads there -- the project's .claude\settings.json or settings.local.json, or ~\.claude\settings.json when the project dir is not this repo -- to declare a hook whose command names the script. Until 2026-10-21 the project-level half was the path test alone, so a deleted hooks block still read ENFORCED. If either half fails the hook is not wired, the rule is emitted as ADVISORY with a note, and the mismatch is listed under 'enforcement'. It does not fail startup: working in JanetHome from another repo's project dir is legitimate, and a brief that tells the truth is worth more than one that refuses to start. Discovered 2026-08-01, when both hook-backed rules read ENFORCED in a session where neither hook was loaded. This comment said 'problems' until 2026-08-14 and was describing the opposite of what the code does: onMissing governs 'problems' and Start-Janet.ps1 treats it as fatal, so routing an unwired hook there is precisely the hard stop the next sentence promises it is not. The separate 'enforcement' field exists for that reason.
$comment.rules.shape: Each rule is { text, why }. 'text' is the imperative and is always emitted; 'why' is the justification and appears only under -Full or -Text. The split keeps the reasoning on disk and reviewable without billing it to every session -- a bare imperative is easier to argue past, which is what the comment above warns against. Plain strings still parse, for anything that does not decompose. Keep 'text' to one line; put the argument in 'why'.
$comment.mcpDependents: The local MCP servers a session can lose, keyed by their name in .mcp.json, each with the 'enforcedBy' of every rule below that cannot keep its promise without that server's tools. Startup reads where a server is switched off for the project dir -- 'disabledMcpjsonServers' in the project's .claude\settings.json or settings.local.json or in ~\.claude\settings.json, and the per-project 'disabledMcpServers' (the /mcp toggle) and 'disabledMcpjsonServers' (a declined .mcp.json approval) in ~\.claude.json -- and for each listed server that is off, relabels the rules named here ADVISORY and adds an 'enforcement' line. A server with no dependent rule is still listed, because losing its tools is worth that line. Every entry must be some rule's enforcedBy, or startup reports a problem: a map naming a script no rule uses would stop relabelling the rule it was meant for without saying so. The graph guard's rule promises a search is answered by mcp__razorgraph__grep; with razorgraph off the session has no such tool. The delegation guard's rule demands mcp__razorgraph__ instructions in a subagent prompt, and since 2026-10-22 the guard stops demanding them where razorgraph is off, so that rule is no longer enforced there either. No ENFORCED rule rests on janet's tools today (the research guard reads a trace Get-Research.ps1 writes, and the CLI still works). Lived in Invoke-JanetStartup.ps1 as $mcpDependents from 2026-10-22 until it moved here the same day; Invoke-DelegationGuard.ps1 reads the same disable state through scripts\lib\McpDisabled.ps1.

rules.text: ENFORCED: never edit research.json directly -- use the research_* MCP tools, 'janet research', or the Add-/Update-ResearchNode scripts.
rules.why: A PreToolUse hook denies Write and Edit against it. All three entry points splice into the file's existing text rather than reserializing it, which is what keeps the hand-curated grouping and comment keys alive; a direct edit is refused because it is the one path with no validation behind it.

rules.text: ENFORCED: fix what the PowerShell linter reports before moving on.
rules.why: A PostToolUse hook lints every .ps1 you write or edit against notes\powershell-house-rules.md.

rules.text: ENFORCED: change a .ps1 or research.json in a repo with Edit/Write (the catalog with janet research), never a shell write -- sed -i, a redirect or heredoc, tee, Set-Content, cp or mv onto it.
rules.why: Every hook that guards an edit -- the edit guard, the lint hook, the research guard -- matches the Write and Edit tools only, so until 2026-10-23 a shell write passed all of them, and the harness's auto mode tells the model to make small edits with sed and heredocs. Lori decided that day that a hook denies them (thread item 7). A PreToolUse hook on Bash and PowerShell now refuses a command that writes research.json, its candidate, previous or base copy, or any .ps1, inside a git working tree; the guarded set is the one those Write|Edit hooks govern, read off their code. git, dotnet and the janet CLI pass, as do reads and writes outside any repo.

rules.text: ENFORCED: startup fails if any manifest entry does not resolve.
rules.why: A broken contract stops the session rather than degrading it quietly.

rules.text: ENFORCED: research first -- ask the catalog before building a tool or hand-rolling a technique.
rules.why: A PreToolUse hook denies Write of a NEW .ps1 into a scripts directory unless Get-Research.ps1 has run recently, and the denial arrives with the closest existing nodes already listed. Written 2026-08-11 after Get-AssemblyApi.ps1 was authored while Get-ApiDoc.ps1 sat in the catalog answering the same question -- nothing was violated, because until now the manifest explained HOW to query the catalog and never said TO. Advisory would not have covered it: 'I only need one type name' is exactly the rationalisation the edit guard was written about.

rules.text: ADVISORY: orchestrate by default -- dispatch work that generates tool output to a subagent and keep the judgement here. The test is VOLUME, not the size of the task.
rules.why: Stated as a standing preference 2026-09-03 ('Orchestrator should be the default at this point'), so the question is not whether a task is big enough to delegate but whether there is a reason it must stay in the main session. A one-line question whose answer needs a repo-wide grep is an agent task; a long piece of reasoning that needs no tools is not. What stays here is what is cheap to state and expensive to get wrong: what a result means, what to do next, what to tell Lori. Written into the manifest 2026-09-07, after a session that dispatched ONE agent and then made about ninety hands-on tool calls -- fixtures, three prose surfaces, verification runs, a cross-repo sweep -- each rationalised as too small or too judgement-heavy to send out, which cumulatively was most of the work. The failure is worth naming precisely, because the instruction already existed and was thorough: note.subagent-delegation carried the doctrine, skills\agent-kickoff carried the template, and Invoke-DelegationGuard.ps1 was wired in both settings files. None of it bound, because every mechanical surface was conditioned on an action the controller was not taking -- the delegation guard fires only on an Agent call that is already happening, the graph guard only on a C#-shaped text search -- and the rules array, the one prose surface every session is guaranteed to read, had never mentioned delegating at all. That absence is what this rule closes. The decision is also not a one-time one: it was made once here, at the start, and never revisited across the rest of the task, which is why Invoke-DelegationGuard.ps1 now also WARNS (never blocks) once a run of consecutive tool calls passes with no dispatch. It warns rather than denies on purpose -- legitimate deep work exists, and a gate that blocks it gets switched off, which is the failure mode the research guard's own reasoning warns about.

rules.text: ENFORCED: a subagent prompt that delegates C# structural work must carry explicit RazorGraph instructions -- the exact mcp__razorgraph__ tool names to load via ToolSearch, the graphId (or the .slnx to build one from), and the graph-first rule itself.
rules.why: Spawned agents inherit the tool surface but not the operating rules: nothing tells them the graph server exists, so they fall back to grep and speculation. Observed 2026-08-11 -- three exploration agents ran text-first until instructed mid-flight; their graph-verified second passes found facts the text passes missed. A PreToolUse hook on the Agent tool now denies such a prompt, and the denial hands back the block already filled in for this repo -- the solution file found on disk and the graphId derived from it -- so clearing it is a paste. Deliberately narrow, on the research guard's own reasoning that a gate firing on everything gets clicked past: it fires only on prompts that look like C# structure, and checks one thing, the presence of mcp__razorgraph__. Escalated from ADVISORY 2026-09-05, when four prompts in one session carried no graph instruction at all while both this rule and skills\agent-kickoff\SKILL.md were in force -- the incident, and the root it shares with the controller's own graph use, are on note.subagent-delegation.

rules.text: ENFORCED: graph first for text search -- a Grep inside a repo is answered by mcp__razorgraph__grep in place of Grep, and any Bash or PowerShell search of files inside a repo, whatever their type, is denied with a paste-ready mcp__razorgraph__grep call; so is a shell read of source (.cs, .razor, .csproj, .sln, .slnx) -- use Read.
rules.why: The delegation guard gates the prompt a subagent is handed; this gates the controller's own hands. Written 2026-09-05 as a gate -- a C#-shaped text search was denied until one of the last 12 tool calls was an mcp__razorgraph__ call -- after four greps for callers and blast radius ran against C# in one session while every graph-first rule was in force (the incident is on note.subagent-delegation). Rewritten 2026-10-11 because the gate taught the wrong lesson: agents cleared it with one throwaway razorgraph call and then grepped anyway, so the graph read as bureaucracy to get past. razorgraph now has grep, which answers from the graph's names and literals and the disk's text in one call, so the hook no longer refuses -- it RUNS the search through razorgraph and returns the results in the denial, and there is nothing left to route around. If the server is down it is started; only if it cannot be started does the hook scan the files itself. Options razorgraph cannot honour (multiline, context lines, a path-shaped glob, an unknown type), an invalid regex, and any hook error let the original Grep through with a one-line note. A path outside any git tree passes untouched; JANET_GRAPH_GUARD=off is the escape hatch. Shell searches are not executed, only redirected, because reading a pattern out of arbitrary shell text rots. Widened 2026-10-12 on Lori's rule, "PowerShell and bash shouldn't be doing searches": the shell trigger stopped being about C#, and a search passes only when it reads another command's output or files outside any repo. Widened again 2026-10-23 (thread item 55, Lori: deny, source only): live probes showed sed -n, cat and Get-Content of a .cs all passing, because a reader counted only when it fed a search. A shell read of .cs, .razor, .csproj, .sln or .slnx inside a repo is now denied and pointed at Read and razorgraph find_nodes; every other file type, and git show, still pass.

rules.text: ADVISORY: graph first, narrative second -- once you know WHAT you are building.
rules.why: Query a semantic model for the narrowest slice that answers the question; read source only to spot-check the claims that matter (DESIGN-NOTES section 4). This is a technique for working inside a problem, and it ranks BELOW research-first: graphing tells you how the code you are about to touch fits together, while the catalog tells you whether to touch it at all. Reaching for the graph -- or worse, for grep -- before asking what already exists is the expensive order.

rules.text: ADVISORY: before an expensive query, name what you are trying to learn and the cheapest query that distinguishes the hypotheses.
rules.why: Agents default to broad exploratory queries that time out or silently truncate. Making hypothesis-formation a prerequisite converts flailing into bisection (section 7).

rules.text: ADVISORY: add a thread item for work you surface but are not doing now; switch focus deliberately, and complete rather than abandon.
rules.why: Debugging is depth-first and working memory is not, so the list is the unwind path. It replaced a push/pop stack on 2026-08-08: adding no longer displaces what is active, items can be amended in place, and completing retains the item instead of deleting it -- so recording work costs nothing and finishing it leaves a record (section 3).

rules.text: ADVISORY: when you wire a value through a seam, pin that the CONSUMER uses it. A test that the value can be read is not a test that it governs, and only a mutation puts the difference beyond doubt.
rules.why: 2026-09-05, gamehub: config/combat.ini's [rates] section was wired through Combat and DemoWorld, tests were added, and the suite went green at 891. Nothing pinned that the world's rates came from the config it was HANDED, so a mutation putting a literal back into GuardRetreatWorld's constructor survived every one of them. The tests proved the value could be read and said nothing about what governed the fight -- the same defect the section already had, one layer up, which is what the work was supposed to fix. General shape: a value has a producer and a consumer, wiring is the edge between them, and asserting on the producer leaves the edge untested. The test that closed it builds the world on a sweep row restating the rates -- the seam's own mechanism rather than a fixture invented for the test, so it keeps working when the seam moves. Found by mutation, not by reading: break the subject, confirm the test fails, restore, report which mutation was used. A survivor is a finding to report, never a test to contrive around. Second dated instance of mutation checks earning their cost, after 2026-09-03 where two tests in one branch were green while proving nothing.

rules.text: ADVISORY: for multi-file mechanical edits, emit a JSON plan and run Invoke-SurgicalEdit.ps1 rather than hand-editing.
rules.why: Models decide well and perform dozens of mechanical edits unreliably. The plan is reviewable before anything touches disk (section 5).

rules.text: ADVISORY: wrap known-flaky external tools in an explicit timeout and fallback.
rules.why: A hung call is indistinguishable from thinking -- the worst failure mode, because it produces no output and no diagnosis (section 8).

rules.text: ADVISORY: nothing employer-SPECIFIC goes in this repo -- their source, their system topology, production telemetry, security-posture detail, colleague personal data. Rebuilding a general pattern from principles is fine even if you first built one there: the test is derivation, not resemblance.
rules.why: Judgement only; no mechanism enforces it, since the identifier list that would is itself employer information. Not a per-edit gate -- the 2026-07-27 extraction settled what was carried over, and the author who made that call is not the risk. The live failure mode is an AGENT with no memory of that decision reproducing something employer-specific from a description. But 'architecture' was too broad a word for that and is gone: this repo's own flagship is a clean-room rebuild (DESIGN-NOTES section 4 -- the Roslyn graph server, employer work product left behind, rebuilt from the pattern), and an SWR cache or an LSP-backed tool is a general technique that belongs to the field, not to whoever you last built one for. PROVENANCE standard 5 already drew the line correctly: 'not coupled to employer systems, and not derived from proprietary internals.' Derivation is the test; resemblance is not evidence of it. PROVENANCE.md is the standard and the record, retrievable as file.provenance.

rules.text: ADVISORY: this machine runs PowerShell 7.x -- invoke scripts with pwsh, write PowerShell 7 syntax, and add -Target Ps51 only when a script may run on stock Windows 5.1 somewhere else.
rules.why: The session shell here is pwsh 7, and nothing in this repo is run or linted with Windows PowerShell 5.1 even though powershell.exe is still present. The hook lints at the Ps7 default, and the 5.1 differences fail in ways that print success. Rules and rationale: notes\powershell-house-rules.md.
